edges.description: Pla-supported airway replication amplifies the bacterial population during the early anti-inflammatory phase of pneumonic plague.
Delayed early inflammation permits unchecked pulmonary bacterial growth before bacterial burden triggers an abrupt pro-inflammatory lung-injury phase.
Infection of the lung manifests clinically as pneumonia.
Fulminant pneumonia can produce bloody sputum and hemoptysis.
Exudative bronchopneumonia produces shortness of breath.
Pulmonary inflammation and airway exudate produce cough.
Fulminant lower-respiratory infection can cause chest pain.
The abrupt pro-inflammatory phase produces systemic fever.
Rapid pulmonary Y. pestis proliferation can progress to bacteremia and systemic septic complications.
Severe septicemic plague can trigger consumptive coagulopathy as a terminal complication.
Severe exudative bronchopneumonia can progress to respiratory failure.

nodes.description: Antimicrobial treatment must be started early because the pneumonic form can be fatal within 48 hours without therapy; aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides all have reported clinical activity in treated human plague, though treated primary pneumonic plague still carried a 27% case fatality rate in published series.

evidence.reference_title: Antimicrobial Treatment of Human Plague: A Systematic Review of the Literature on Individual Cases, 1937-2019.
evidence.snippet: In addition to aminoglycosides, other classes of antimicrobials including tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides are effective for plague treatment, although publication bias and low numbers in certain treatment groups may limit interpretation.

evidence.reference_title: Antimicrobial Treatment Patterns and Illness Outcome Among United States Patients With Plague, 1942-2018.
evidence.snippet: Mortality differed significantly among those receiving high-efficacy therapy (9%) and only limited-efficacy therapy (51%).
